sub: Sorting the painful scrotum, the swelling that glows and the painless lump, from torsion and epididymitis to seminoma and its markers.

pretest.q: Which bedside finding best separates testicular torsion from epididymitis?
pretest.why: Torsion abolishes the cremasteric reflex in nearly every case, while epididymitis leaves it intact. Redness, warmth and swelling occur with both conditions, so they cannot tell them apart.

w.Scrotal redness: Erythema appears with any inflamed or ischemic scrotum, so it shows up in twisting and infection alike and cannot separate the two.
w.Fever: Fever is somewhat more typical of infection, but it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to rule a twisted cord in or out.
w.Scrotal swelling: Edema of the scrotal wall follows both a twisted cord and an infected epididymis, so the size of the swelling points to neither one.

pretest.q: Which serum marker does a pure seminoma never raise?
pretest.why: Seminoma cells lack yolk sac differentiation, so they never make AFP; a raised AFP means a nonseminomatous component. Seminoma can mildly raise hCG and LDH, and its cells express placental alkaline phosphatase.

w.Human chorionic gonadotropin: Scattered syncytiotrophoblast cells within some seminomas release small amounts of hCG, so a mild rise is compatible with seminoma.
w.Lactate dehydrogenase: LDH rises with tumor bulk in any germ cell tumor, including bulky seminoma, so it reflects stage rather than tumor type.
w.Placental alkaline phosphatase: PLAP is expressed by seminoma cells and germ cell neoplasia in situ, so it is a marker that supports seminoma rather than excluding it.

pretest.q: Why do varicoceles form far more often on the left side?
o: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein
The left testicular artery arises from the renal artery
The left inguinal canal is wider than the right
The left testis lies higher in the scrotum
pretest.why: The left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, adding a long, high-pressure column of blood, whereas the right vein enters the inferior vena cava obliquely and rarely backs up.

w.The left testicular artery arises from t: Both testicular arteries usually arise from the aorta, and a varicocele is a venous problem, so arterial origin cannot explain it.
w.The left inguinal canal is wider than th: Canal width matters for indirect hernias, not for venous pressure in the pampiniform plexus, and the two canals are similar.
w.The left testis lies higher in the scrot: The left testis usually hangs slightly lower, and its position does not raise pressure in the veins that drain it.

body: Why does an undescended testis carry risks for life?

The fetal testis forms on the posterior abdominal wall and descends in two phases: INSL3 from Leydig cells swells the gubernaculum and holds the testis near the inguinal ring, and androgens then drive it through the inguinal canal behind the {{rp20procvag|processus vaginalis}}, a finger of peritoneum whose lower end remains after descent as the tunica vaginalis. **Cryptorchidism**, a testis that fails to reach the scrotum, is the most common congenital genital anomaly in boys, seen in about 3 percent of term and up to 30 percent of preterm boys, and most descend by 6 months. A {{rp20retractile|retractile testis}} is normal: a brisk cremasteric reflex pulls it up, but it comes down easily and stays down. An ascending testis was once low and rises later, and a truly undescended testis cannot be brought down. **Orchiopexy** between 6 and 18 months makes the testis examinable and helps fertility.

The complications come from heat and from dysgenesis. A testis at body temperature loses germ cells within the first year, and infertility is worst with **bilateral cryptorchidism**. A **germ cell tumor**, most often seminoma, becomes several times more likely, and not only in the undescended testis: the contralateral, descended testis is also at higher risk, which shows that the defect lies in the testis and not only in its position. An undescended testis twists more easily, and the patent processus vaginalis that often accompanies it is a route for an **inguinal hernia**. A bilateral, nonpalpable pair of testes, especially with hypospadias, is a disorder of sex development until shown otherwise and needs a karyotype, 17-hydroxyprogesterone and electrolytes.
Orchiopexy lowers the cancer risk but never removes it

Fixing the position does not fix the gonad. Cryptorchidism reflects testicular dysgenesis, so the risk of germ cell tumors, most often **seminoma**, stays raised in the repaired testis and in the other one. An undescended testis shows a thick tubular basement membrane, loss of spermatogonia and, in some cases, {{rp20gcnis|germ cell neoplasia in situ}}, the precursor lesion.
Is this painful scrotum torsion or epididymitis?

Testicular **torsion** happens when the testis rotates and twists its spermatic cord. The usual setup in adolescents is the {{rp20bellclap|bell-clapper deformity}}: the tunica vaginalis attaches too high, so the testis hangs free; neonatal torsion has no such defect. Twisting compresses the thin-walled veins before the thicker arteries, so blood enters but cannot leave; venous congestion swells the testis, which then undergoes **hemorrhagic infarction**. The typical patient has sudden, severe pain, nausea and vomiting, a high-riding testis with a horizontal lie and an absent {{rp20cremreflex|cremasteric reflex}}, and sometimes earlier pain that resolved on its own, which suggests intermittent torsion. The reflex runs through the genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2): stroking the inner thigh signals up its femoral branch, and its genital branch makes the cremaster lift the ipsilateral testis.

**Epididymitis** is infection that climbs from the urethra along the ductus deferens. In sexually active men younger than about 35, the usual causes are Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae; in older men with obstruction or instrumentation, and in men who have insertive anal sex, enteric rods such as Escherichia coli dominate. Pain builds over days, the epididymis is tender, lifting the testis eases the pain (a positive {{rp20prehn|Prehn sign}}), the reflex is preserved and Doppler shows increased flow. CDC treatment is ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, or levofloxacin when enteric organisms are likely. A torsed appendix testis, a remnant at the upper pole, causes focal pain and a blue dot in boys of about 7 to 12.
Torsion is a clinical diagnosis on a clock

Salvage is above 90 percent when the cord is untwisted within 6 hours, about 50 percent at 12 hours and below 10 percent after 24 hours. A boy with sudden pain, a high-riding testis and no cremasteric reflex goes to the operating room; **Doppler** can support the diagnosis but must not delay surgery. Manual **detorsion**, rotating the testis outward like opening a book, can buy time but never replaces surgery. The surgeon untwists the cord and performs **bilateral orchiopexy**, because the bell-clapper defect is usually bilateral.
What else makes a testis hurt, and in what order is it worked up?

Testicular pain is not always testicular. A **ureteral stone** can refer pain to the testis because the ureter and the testis share spinal sensory levels, and an incarcerated inguinal hernia can do the same, so the flank, abdomen and groin are examined too. Blunt trauma can rupture the testis, orchitis swells and tenderizes the whole gland, Fournier gangrene causes pain out of proportion to the exam with crepitus in the perineum, and a firm painless intratesticular mass is a tumor until proven otherwise. The work-up follows the exam: check the reflex and the lie first, send a urinalysis and a urethral nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) when infection is likely, and use Doppler ultrasound to confirm torsion or to show the increased flow of epididymo-orchitis.
What inflames the testis itself, and why can mumps cause infertility?

**Orchitis** is inflammation of the testis proper. The classic cause is **mumps**, which inflames the testis in roughly 20 to 30 percent of males infected after puberty, usually about a week after the parotitis. The swollen testis is trapped inside the unyielding tunica albuginea, so pressure rises and the seminiferous tubules undergo pressure necrosis and atrophy, and damage to the blood-testis barrier adds an immune attack; bilateral disease can leave a man infertile. A breach of that barrier by trauma, vasectomy or infection also exposes sperm antigens to the immune system and can cause autoimmune orchitis. **Granulomatous** orchitis takes two main forms: tuberculosis, which usually starts in the epididymis and forms caseating granulomas, and an idiopathic, probably autoimmune form in middle-aged men that presents as a firm mass mimicking a tumor.
Which scrotal swellings glow with light, and which one signals a kidney tumor?

A **hydrocele** is serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis around the testis; it is smooth and painless, and it **transilluminates**. In infants, a communicating hydrocele means the processus vaginalis stayed open, so peritoneal fluid moves in and out and the swelling changes size; a wide opening allows an indirect hernia, and most infant hydroceles close by 12 to 24 months. Adult hydroceles are usually noncommunicating and can react to infection, trauma or tumor, so every new one gets an ultrasound. Where filariasis is endemic, filarial worms block the scrotal lymphatics and the sac fills with milky lymph, a chylocele, which can also transilluminate. A spermatocele, or epididymal cyst, sits above and behind the testis, separate from it, and also transilluminates. An indirect inguinal hernia is the swelling you cannot get above, because it runs up into the inguinal canal and shows an impulse on coughing.

Blood in the tunica vaginalis after trauma is a **hematocele**; it stays dark and does not transilluminate. Blunt trauma that tears the tunica albuginea is a testicular rupture, with extrusion of seminiferous tubules: ultrasound shows a heterogeneous testis, loss of its contour and a break in the capsule, and exploration within 72 hours saves most testes, whereas delay ends in orchiectomy. A large hematocele alone does not make the diagnosis, so the testis itself is imaged.

A **varicocele** is a tangle of dilated pampiniform veins in the spermatic cord, felt above the testis as a **bag of worms** that fills on standing and empties when the man lies down; grade I is seen only with Valsalva, grade II is palpable and grade III is visible. It is found in about 15 percent of men and about 40 percent of men with primary infertility. About 90 percent are left-sided, because the left testicular vein joins the left renal vein at a right angle, a longer, higher-pressure route, while the right drains obliquely into the inferior vena cava. The pooled warm blood impairs spermatogenesis, making varicocele the most common surgically correctable cause of male infertility, although one seen only on ultrasound is not repaired. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that stays full when supine, suggests a mass blocking venous return, such as **renal cell** carcinoma in the vena cava, so the abdomen is imaged.
How do testicular tumors differ, and which markers name them?

A testicular tumor classically presents in a man aged 15 to 35 as a **painless**, firm mass within the testis that does not transilluminate; ultrasound shows a solid **intratesticular** lesion. It is the most common solid cancer in men of this age and is highly curable, so delay is the enemy. Risk factors are cryptorchidism in either testis, a tumor in the other testis, a family history and infertility, because cryptorchidism, hypospadias, poor spermatogenesis and germ cell tumor share one fetal dysgenesis. About 95 percent of tumors are germ cell tumors, which usually arise from germ cell neoplasia in situ and carry an isochromosome 12p.

Seminoma, the most common single type, peaks in the 30s and 40s. It forms a homogeneous gray-white, fleshy mass of large fried-egg cells with clear cytoplasm, divided by fibrous septa full of lymphocytes; its cells express placental alkaline phosphatase and often carry KIT mutations. Seminoma never makes AFP, can mildly raise hCG and is very sensitive to radiation and chemotherapy.

Nonseminomatous germ cell tumors are usually mixed and more aggressive. **Embryonal carcinoma** forms a hemorrhagic, necrotic mass of primitive, pleomorphic cells and may raise AFP or hCG. **Yolk sac tumor** is the most common testicular tumor in boys younger than 3; it secretes AFP and shows {{rp20schiller|Schiller-Duval bodies}}. **Choriocarcinoma**, made of syncytiotrophoblast and cytotrophoblast, spreads early through the blood to the lungs and brain and makes very high hCG, which causes gynecomastia and, by stimulating the TSH receptor, hyperthyroidism. Teratoma contains tissues of all three germ layers; in adult men even mature-looking teratoma can metastasize.
AFP normal; hCG normal or mildly raised
Tissue from all three germ layers
AFP raised in some; malignant potential in adult men
Small, medium and large cells, no lymphocytes
No marker; not from GCNIS; usually benign

About 5 percent of testicular tumors arise from sex cord-stromal cells and make hormones rather than markers. A **Leydig cell tumor** is a golden-brown nodule of eosinophilic cells with rod-shaped Reinke crystals; its androgens cause precocious puberty in boys, and their conversion to estrogen causes gynecomastia in men, while AFP and hCG stay normal; it is not associated with germ cell neoplasia in situ or isochromosome 12p. Most are benign, and Sertoli cell tumors are usually hormonally silent. In men older than 60 the most common testicular mass is **lymphoma**, usually diffuse large B-cell type and often bilateral. Testicular tumors spread first to the **para-aortic** lymph nodes near the renal vessels, while choriocarcinoma spreads through the blood.
Working up a painless testicular lump
A firm mass within the testis that blocks light is treated as cancer until proven otherwise, while a cystic swelling that glows points to fluid.
Ultrasound confirms a solid intratesticular lesion and separates it from a hydrocele, spermatocele or varicocele outside the testis.
Markers drawn before surgery suggest the tumor type, contribute to staging and give a baseline for follow-up after removal.
The testis and cord are removed through the groin with high ligation of the cord; a scrotal biopsy is avoided, and sperm banking is offered first.

CT of the abdomen and chest looks for lymph node spread (right-sided tumors reach interaortocaval nodes first, left-sided tumors the left para-aortic nodes) and lung spread; markers that fall more slowly than their half-lives (hCG about a day, AFP 5 to 7 days) signal residual disease.
A high AFP means the tumor is not a pure seminoma

Pure seminoma never secretes **AFP**. If a tumor reported as seminoma comes with a raised AFP, it contains a nonseminomatous component, usually yolk sac tumor, and it is treated as a nonseminomatous tumor. A mildly raised **hCG** fits seminoma, because scattered syncytiotrophoblast cells make it; only very high hCG points to choriocarcinoma. LDH is nonspecific and tracks tumor bulk, so it helps with prognosis, not with typing.
How is each scrotal condition treated?
Observe in infants, since most close by 12 to 24 months; repair if it persists or a hernia accompanies it. Adults need a hydrocelectomy only if it is large or painful.
Observe; excise only if large or painful, because surgery can scar the epididymis.
Observe if painless with normal semen. Varicocelectomy or embolization for pain, infertility with abnormal semen, or loss of testicular size in an adolescent.
Mumps orchitis is supportive (scrotal support, NSAIDs, ice); bacterial orchitis gets the epididymitis antibiotics; tuberculosis gets antituberculous drugs.
Sperm banking, then radical inguinal orchiectomy.
Stage I: surveillance, one dose of carboplatin or para-aortic radiation. Advanced disease: cisplatin-based chemotherapy.
Low-risk stage I: surveillance. Otherwise BEP (bleomycin, etoposide, cisplatin), then retroperitoneal lymph node dissection for any residual mass, because teratoma resists chemotherapy.

body.q: A 61-year-old man has a new right-sided varicocele that stays full when he lies down. Which reasoning best guides the next step?
o: Right-sided varicoceles are the common kind because the right testicular vein is longer, so reassurance is enough
The right testicular vein drains straight into the inferior vena cava, so a new right varicocele that does not empty suggests a mass blocking venous return
A swelling that stays full when he is supine must be a hydrocele, so transillumination is the key test
Varicoceles come from arterial malformations, so Doppler of the testicular artery will settle the diagnosis
body.why: Varicoceles are usually left-sided because the left testicular vein enters the left renal vein at a right angle, giving a long, high-pressure column. The right vein enters the inferior vena cava obliquely and rarely backs up. A new right-sided varicocele, or one that stays full lying flat, therefore implies obstruction downstream, classically renal cell carcinoma growing into the vena cava, so the abdomen is imaged.

body: Why must a suspected testicular cancer be removed through the groin rather than the scrotum?

The testis develops near the kidney and drags its vessels and lymphatics with it as it descends, so its lymph drains to para-aortic nodes at the level of the renal vessels, whereas scrotal skin drains to superficial inguinal nodes. Cutting through the scrotum could spill tumor into the scrotal wall and open that second nodal route, complicating staging and treatment. A radical inguinal orchiectomy removes the testis and cord through the groin and ties the cord high, so the tumor never touches the scrotal lymphatics.

grid.q: Which of these point toward testicular torsion rather than epididymitis?
items: High-riding testis with a horizontal lie
Bell-clapper attachment of the tunica vaginalis
Pain relieved by lifting the testis
Tender swollen epididymis with an intact reflex
